mc_quote: Digger is a grandiose folly of a film, a failure on its own perhaps impossible-to-satisfy terms.

Iñárritu’s grand black comedy initially seems like a modern Dr. Strangelove—a bleak satire of the end of the world caused by not atomic but environmental catastrophe. But it doesn’t take long for the filmmaker to reveal his conceit.
To be as generous to Digger as possible, it feels like an Armando Iannucci rewrite away from being a masterpiece. But that distance is nonetheless as vast as a civilization-blitzing ice shelf.
An unrecognizable, Oscar-ready Tom Cruise is eager to show what he’s got as a paunchy, preening, tantrum-throwing Texas oil powerbroker.  He’s got plenty. The movie not so much.

The relative restraint and expressive specificity of Plemons’s performance — his character holds his gaze on other people a touch too long, and his smile seems backlit by madness — is a relief, given the rest of the cast’s cartoony turns. It’s a bummer to see actors like Goodman, Stuhlbarg and Riz Ahmed so badly handled.
Seldom have I encountered a greater disjunction between the bludgeoning overkill of a film’s verbiage and the playful sublimity of its visuals. Iñárritu’s technique transcends gimmickry.
It’s less about politics and more about the function of art in crisis, yet remains oddly toothless for a film so insistent it’s making some sort of pronouncement.

Digger, the eighth feature film from Alejandro G. Iñárritu, is pure, empty-headed trickery, a drab-looking gewgaw with a million moving parts and nothing to say, even if it desperately claws at profundity every minute.
Cruise is digging for that Oscar win with a performance well outside of his wheelhouse, but in terms of sheer cinematic entertainment, “Digger” is one dry well.
The mess isn’t even hot here; it’s as ice cold as the filmmakers think their satire is, and as devastatingly bad as the cataclysmic climate control crisis at the center of its plot.

The director and Cruise, as well as the crew and supporting cast...have purposefully given us something messy, ungainly, clever to a fault, and designed to play like a shriek of rage and pain. It’s impossible to simply dismiss as a mistake, and equally impossible to declare that it works in almost any capacity.

For all the film’s crazy performances, its directorial grandstanding, its wildly miscalculated rug-pulling, a genuine current of civilizational despair runs through Digger. That sadness, that horror, serves as Iñárritu’s ultimate justification, and this time, it’s a compelling one. Somewhere behind that camera, he acknowledges that he is just as lost as the rest of us.
Digger chokes on its own ambitions, and very few of the picture’s participants emerge still breathing.

Risky art is often called a high-wire act, but Tom Cruise’s latest film really earns the label. Until it took its very last step, I honestly couldn’t have told you whether it was going to come off or splat headfirst into the sawdust.

Digger lacks emotional depth, being much more interested in the showmanship of tricks and razzle-dazzle than character development. While Cruise puts on a good show, he’s walking around the loose threads of the script to get there.

Tom Cruise takes enormous risks playing the outlandish title character, and his daring portrait of avarice and ego is occasionally striking in its ferocity. But this ambitious misfire is consistently sabotaged by Iñárritu’s gratingly unsubtle comedic approach – not to mention his introduction of a meta twist that further alienates the audience.

But when you’re watching a film that doesn’t really seem to work, which then voluntarily indulges the suggestion that its very existence might be completely pointless – well, then, why did any of us, filmmaker or audience, bother in the first place?
There is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you’re in a hole?

Here’s the real problem: “Digger” isn’t funny. It’s nervy, in your face, adventurous, and bizarro in a free-swinging, out-of-the-box way. And it feels like a comedy, since it’s fueled by the relentless overacting of a bad Coen brothers movie. But “Dr. Strangelove,” built around the genius of Peter Sellers, was brilliantly funny. “Digger” borrows the doomsday architecture of “Strangelove” but leaves out the slyness, replacing it with a lavishly overscaled spectacle of browbeating.
